also: he must always have his own way

evidence: Ter. Ph. 950: Nōlō, volō; volō, nōlō rūrsum
Cic. Att. 12.41.1: scīre tamen volēbam ubi essēs
Traupman 211, 212: Velim comparāre tesseram, I’d like to buy a ticket
terms.comment: With an infinitive (scīre volēbam), an accusative and infinitive (tē venīre volō) or a bare subjunctive (quid faciam vīs?, Hor. Ep. 2.2.57). Vīn', for vīsne, offers something; the polite velim is “I’d like”.
“I don’t want” is normally nōlō; nōlī with an infinitive is “don’t!”.

evidence: Cic. Fam. 14.4.1: ego vērō tē quam prīmum, mea vīta, cupiō vidēre
terms.comment: Stronger than volō: the word of Cicero’s letters for longing to see someone.

evidence: Plaut. Most. 1131: ego ībō prō tē, sī tibi nōn libet
Traupman 98: libuit; quia mihi libitum est
terms.comment: With a dative of the person: nōn libet, “I don’t feel like it”; ut libet, “as you like”. Comedy often spells it lubet.

phrases.latin: Nōlō, volō; volō, nōlō rūrsum; cedo, cape.
phrases.english: I don’t want it, I want it; I want it, then I don’t; give it here, take it.
What do you want me to do?
I don’t want you to hurry.

phrases.latin: quam tarda es! inquit; nōn vīs citius prōgredī?
phrases.english: “How slow you are!” he said. “Won’t you go faster?”

phrases.latin: ego eō ad forum, nisi quid vīs.
phrases.english: I’m off to the forum, unless you want something.
He must always have his own way.
I’d like to buy a pet.
